metadata.title: Public and private school efficiency and equity in Latin America: New evidence based on PISA for development

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA for Development (PISA-D) 2017 microdata merged across student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires, then aggregates variables to the school level for DEA. The paper does not report the use of PISA-D sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the DEA or the second-stage regressions, and it does not name any weight variable (such as TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the main estimation is Data Envelopment Analysis with bootstrap bias correction (Simar & Wilson approach), the uncertainty quantification relies on bootstrapping rather than survey-weighted variance estimation. Analysts should therefore treat the results as efficiency comparisons based on the available school sample (705 schools) without explicit complex-survey weighting adjustments, unless weights are applied in the underlying OECD PISA-D data preparation not described here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are used for cognitive outcomes: the DEA outputs are mean school values for math, reading, and science scores, using the first plausible value (out of 10) for each subject. The paper does not describe how missing data were handled when constructing the merged school-level dataset and the DEA inputs/outputs, so the missing-data strategy cannot be verified from the text. This is a reporting gap because PISA-D datasets typically contain item nonresponse and missing questionnaire responses that can affect school-level aggregates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis is based on PISA-D 2017 for lower- and middle-income countries, restricted to four Latin American countries: Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Paraguay. The working sample is constructed by merging three PISA-D questionnaires (students, teachers, and school/principal) and then aggregating variables to the school level. The DEA is run on 705 schools total (207 private, 498 public), using school-level averages of cognitive outcomes (math, reading, science) and school-level inputs (family SES, school infrastructure indices, student–teacher ratio inverse). For the second-stage regressions, the authors use the estimated DEA efficiency scores as dependent variables and include environmental covariates derived from student, teacher, and school characteristics (Table 2 and Tables B1/B2), with separate models for the whole sample and for private-only and public-only school subsamples.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged Family SES (escs15), Physical infrastructure index, Educational infrastructure index to predict science scores, finding that This study uses PISA for Development (PISA-D) 2017 data for four Latin American countries—Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Paraguay—restricted to students at grade 7 (15 years old) or above, then merged across student, teacher, and school/principal questionnaires. The analysis is conducted at the school level (705 schools: 207 private, 498 public) using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with outputs defined as school mean math, reading, and science scores based on the first plausible value (PV1) for each subject. Technical efficiency is estimated with variable returns to scale and bias-corrected via homogeneous bootstrapping (2000 repetitions), yielding mean bias-corrected efficiency of 0.88 for private schools and 0.82 for public schools in the pooled region. Second-stage regressions (Simar–Wilson two-stage DEA) relate efficiency to student, teacher, and school characteristics and to inequality/policy indicators. The paper does not report a missing-data handling strategy and does not describe the use of PISA-D sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as efficiency comparisons based on the constructed school sample rather than fully survey-weighted population estimates. data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an efficiency/equity study using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and two-stage DEA regressions rather than machine-learning prediction. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques is empty) and no predictive target-variable performance metrics (main_findings is left empty). The study’s outcomes are efficiency scores and their determinants, reported through DEA bootstrap estimates and regression coefficients rather than ML accuracy/RMSE/AUC metrics.
